english: hello; thanks for your hard work (between coworkers)
use: The all-purpose work greeting: passing a coworker, starting a call or message, coming back to the office.

example.romaji: Otsukaresama desu. Kaigi, mou hajimatte imasu ka?
example.ja: お疲れ様です。会議、もう始まっていますか？
example.english: Hi. Has the meeting started yet?

notes: Friends say otsukare after a club, a shift or a long day.

english: good work today; thanks for your hard work
use: Said when work or an event ends, especially to someone leaving; the answer to osaki ni shitsurei shimasu.

example.romaji: Kyou wa nagai ichinichi deshita ne. Otsukaresama deshita.
example.ja: 今日は長い一日でしたね。お疲れ様でした。

notes: Casual: otsukare. Also said after a match, a show or a long trip.

english: thanks for your trouble (to workers, juniors)
use: Said to delivery drivers, guards or juniors doing a job for you; not to your boss.

example.english: Thanks for coming out in the cold.

notes: Said upward it sounds bossy; to anyone above you, use otsukaresama desu.

english: thanks for your trouble; good job
use: Casual thanks from a boss or older person to someone below them; you'll mostly hear it.

example.romaji: Kyou wa gokurousan. Mou agatte ii yo.
example.ja: 今日はご苦労さん。もう上がっていいよ。
example.english: Thanks for today. You can head home now.

examplePolite.english: Thanks for coming out in the rain.

notes: Only from higher to lower; never say it to your boss.

use: A host greets a visitor at the door, or a small shop owner greets customers; the guest answers ojama shimasu.

example.ja: いらっしゃい！寒かったでしょう、入って。
example.english: Welcome! You must be cold, come in.

examplePolite.ja: いらっしゃいませ。何名様ですか？
examplePolite.english: Welcome. How many in your party?

notes: Shop staff's irasshaimase needs no reply; a nod is fine.

use: A host invites you up from the entryway into the house; take your shoes off and say ojama shimasu.

example.romaji: Douzo, oagari kudasai. Surippa, kochira desu.
example.ja: どうぞ、お上がりください。スリッパ、こちらです。
example.english: Please, come on in. Here are some slippers.

notes: Casual: agatte, agatte. Agaru is stepping up from the entryway.

use: A host tells a guest to sit however they like, often to someone kneeling formally.

example.romaji: Ashi kuzushite, raku ni shite ne.
example.english: Stretch your legs out, make yourself comfortable.

examplePolite.romaji: Douzo oraku ni. Ocha iremasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: どうぞお楽に。お茶入れますね。
examplePolite.english: Please, make yourself comfortable. I'll make some tea.

notes: Doctors say it too: raku ni shite kudasai (relax).

use: Staff, hosts or interviewers invite you to sit; say shitsurei shimasu as you sit down.

example.ja: どうぞ、こちらにおかけください。

notes: Casual: suwatte. In waiting rooms you'll hear okake ni natte omachi kudasai.

use: Said by a guest stepping into someone's home or office, or joining a group.

example.romaji: Ojama shimasu. Kore, minna de tabete kudasai.
example.ja: お邪魔します。これ、みんなで食べてください。
example.english: Thanks for having me. Here's something for everyone.

notes: Friends just say ojama. Plain jama means 'in the way', and jama da! is rude.

use: Said by a guest at the door when leaving someone's home; the host answers mata kite ne.

example.romaji: Kyou wa ojama shimashita. Tanoshikatta desu.
example.ja: 今日はお邪魔しました。楽しかったです。
example.english: Thanks for having me today. It was fun.

notes: The pair: ojama shimasu coming in, ojama shimashita going out.

use: A host or friend urging you to eat, sit or ask for something; accept with jaa, enryo naku.

example.romaji: Takusan aru kara, enryo shinaide tabete.
example.ja: たくさんあるから、遠慮しないで食べて。
example.english: There's plenty, so don't be shy, eat up.

examplePolite.romaji: Takusan arimasu kara, goenryo naku douzo.
examplePolite.ja: たくさんありますから、ご遠慮なくどうぞ。
examplePolite.english: There's plenty, so please help yourself.

notes: Enryo is holding back out of politeness; guests decline once, so hosts insist.

politeJa: 遠慮なくいただきます
english: without holding back; I'll gladly take it
use: Said when accepting an offer after the host insists, or to urge someone: enryo naku itte (just tell me).

example.romaji: Jaa, enryo naku moratte iku ne.
example.ja: じゃあ、遠慮なくもらっていくね。
example.english: Well then, I'll gladly take it.

examplePolite.ja: では、遠慮なくいただきます。

english: please don't go to any trouble
use: A guest's polite line when the host offers tea or food.

example.romaji: A, douzo okamai naku. Sugu kaerimasu kara.
example.ja: あ、どうぞおかまいなく。すぐ帰りますから。
example.english: Oh, please don't trouble yourself. I'm leaving soon.

notes: The host usually brings tea anyway; just thank them.

use: Letting someone go first at a door, lift or till; they answer sumimasen or doumo.

example.romaji: Watashi wa ato de ii kara, osaki ni douzo.
example.ja: 私は後でいいから、お先にどうぞ。
example.english: I can go later, so go ahead.

examplePolite.romaji: Watashi wa ato de daijoubu desu kara, osaki ni douzo.
examplePolite.ja: 私は後で大丈夫ですから、お先にどうぞ。
examplePolite.english: I'm fine going later, so please go ahead.

notes: A host may also offer you the bath first with it.

use: Light polite apology for a small slip: bumping someone, a wrong number, walking into the wrong room.

example.romaji: A, heya o machigaemashita. Shitsurei shimashita.
example.ja: あ、部屋を間違えました。失礼しました。

notes: Shitsurei shimasu (present) is for entering, leaving or hanging up.

english: I'm getting off (on a crowded train or bus)
use: Said aloud to the people in your way as your stop comes, so they make room.

example.ja: すみません、降ります！ちょっと通してください。
example.english: Excuse me, getting off! Let me through, please.

notes: From oriru (get off). In a crowd, sumimasen alone also works.

use: Opens a personal or awkward question to someone you don't know well, like their name, age or company.

example.romaji: Shitsurei desu ga, otoshi wa oikutsu desu ka?
example.ja: 失礼ですが、お年はおいくつですか？
example.english: Excuse me for asking, but how old are you?

notes: Not for getting someone's attention; use sumimasen for that.
